analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to force recalls, subpoena witnesses, and fine companies that violate food and drug safety law.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: after subcommittee hearings and a mark-up, a rewritten version (H.R. 3642) was forwarded to the full Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the FDA's enforcement powers over food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices. It would have let the agency — or a federal court — order companies to recall dangerous or fraudulent products, given the FDA commissioner subpoena power for investigations, imposed civil fines of up to $1 million per violation (including for bribery of FDA officials and obstruction of investigations), broadened factory inspections, and tightened rules on tainted imports, including mandatory destruction of imported goods that pose a significant health risk.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices — essentially everyone. The bill aimed to get unsafe or fraudulent products off shelves faster, by letting the FDA order mandatory recalls instead of relying on voluntary company cooperation, by penalizing companies up to $1 million per violation for infractions including false statements and obstructing FDA investigations, and by blocking risky imports at the border.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of food, drugs, and cosmetics

how_it_helps.text: Any U.S. district court could order a manufacturer, importer, distributor, or retailer to recall a product whose violation involves fraud or a significant risk to human or animal health.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services could order mandatory recalls for the same reasons, with the order constituting final agency action, and companies would have to report any recall they initiated within 5 days.
The FDA Commissioner would gain subpoena power for hearings, investigations, and standard-setting, with court enforcement for refusal to comply.

Civil money penalties of up to $250,000 for individuals and $1,000,000 for other persons per violation would apply to violating the Act, making false statements, bribery of Department officials, destroying evidence, and obstructing investigations.

FDA inspections could extend to all things bearing on a violation — equipment, materials, records, processes, and facilities — with authority to retain samples and copy records, and regulated firms would have to keep records and make reports as the Secretary determines necessary.

Articles offered for import in violation of the law could be refused admission; imported articles posing a significant health risk would have to be destroyed within 30 days, without an option to relabel or export, and import bonds would have to equal at least three times invoice value.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors of FDA-regulated products, who would face mandatory recall orders, broader inspections and record-keeping requirements, subpoena exposure, and civil fines of up to $1 million per violation for wrongdoing including fraud, bribery of regulators, and obstruction. Consumers would indirectly bear some compliance costs passed into prices.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory recall authority, expanded inspections, and record-keeping requirements impose real compliance costs on regulated companies, some of which would likely be passed to consumers in prices.

The bill's civil penalty and enforcement structure leaves the Secretary substantial discretion in assessing fines, and the bill would have replaced existing device-specific civil penalty provisions, raising fair-notice questions for smaller firms.

Automatic destruction within 30 days of refused-import articles posing a significant health risk — without the option to relabel or export — is a severe remedy for cases where the health-risk finding may be contested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — faster removal of dangerous or fraudulent food, drugs, and devices and tougher penalties for deceiving regulators — plausibly outweighed compliance costs, which fell mainly on firms whose products violated the law. The strongest honest objection is the cost and rigidity of some remedies (mandatory destruction of contested imports, sweeping inspection and record-keeping mandates), but these targeted serious violations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 1991 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; its Health and the Environment Subcommittee held hearings and a mark-up, and on October 24, 1991 forwarded a clean bill, H.R. 3642, in lieu of the original — but the full committee never acted and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 7, 1991 by Rep. Henry Waxman (with Rep. John Dingell) and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on June 24, 1991, which held hearings on July 17, 1991 and a consideration and mark-up session on October 10, 1991.
On October 24, 1991, the subcommittee forwarded a clean bill, H.R. 3642, to the full committee in lieu of H.R. 2597.
No further action was taken; the full committee never marked up or reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: FDA-regulated manufacturers, importers, and distributors of food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices — they avoided mandatory recall authority, subpoena power, expanded inspections, and civil fines of up to $1 million per violation that Congress never enacted.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, Health and the Environment Subcommittee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and advanced it through his subcommittee's hearings and mark-up, sending a clean bill to the full committee.

for.name: Rep. John Dingell
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original sponsor of the bill at introduction.

for.name: Reps. Flake and Rangel
for.what_they_did: Signed on as additional sponsors in September 1991.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a mark-up or reported the rewritten bill (H.R. 3642) to the House floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Food, drug, cosmetic, and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to mandatory recall orders, court-ordered recalls, subpoena power, expanded inspections and record-keeping mandates, and civil fines of up to $1 million per violation, including for false statements, bribery of FDA officials, and obstruction of investigations. The bill died before reaching a floor vote, so these requirements never took effect.

The bill would have required refusal of admission for any article in violation of the law, mandatory destruction within 30 days of articles posing a significant health risk (without option to relabel or export), bonds of at least three times invoice value, and marking of refused articles before export.
